content:
Yesterday we looked at the four types of animals in the peace offering; the oxen, the rams, the male goats, and the lambs of the first year and we saw how the four types together declare that the peace of Christ extends to every corner of the earth, to every tribe and language and people and nation. Today we take one step back and look at the peace offering not by type but by total count. When we add all four types together; two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five male lambs we get seventeen animals per leader. Seventeen animals of peace. And the number seventeen, when we trace it through Scripture, has a message of its own that brings everything we have been studying in the peace offering into sharp and beautiful focus.

Genesis 8:4 records a detail “In the seventh month, the seventeenth day of the month, the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat.” The waters of the flood had covered the earth. The judgment of Yahweh had fallen on a world that had filled itself with violence and corruption. Everything outside the ark had been swept away. And then, on the seventeenth day of the seventh month, the ark came to rest. Not on the fifteenth, not on the twentieth; the seventeenth. Judgment had run its full course. Deliverance was secured. The new beginning was established. The ark rested on seventeen.

This is where the number seventeen first speaks in Scripture, and it speaks of one thing clearly: victory on the other side of judgment. Not victory that avoided the flood, but victory that came through it. The ark did not bypass the judgment. It carried the people through it. And when the waters began to recede and the ark settled on solid ground, the number written on that day was seventeen. The peace offering total of seventeen animals per leader is standing in this same light. Each tribal leader brought seventeen animals of peace to the altar; not before the judgment had been dealt with, but after the sin offering. And then seventeen animals of peace symbolized that the Judgment has ended. Deliverance is secured. Peace is established.

There is a second appearance of seventeen in Scripture that deepens the picture significantly. Genesis 37:2 says: “Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers.” The story that follows is one of the most detailed and spiritually layered type-antitypes of Christ in all of the Old Testament. At seventeen, Joseph received prophetic dreams that showed his brothers and even his parents bowing down before him. At seventeen, the dreams were given that marked out his destiny. And at seventeen, the suffering that would eventually lead to the fulfillment of those dreams began.
His brothers hated him. They stripped him of his coat. They threw him into a pit. They sold him for silver. And at seventeen years old, Joseph the dreamer began the long, painful journey through the pit, through slavery, through false accusation, through prison, before he arrived at the throne room of Egypt.

Joseph is one of the clearest types of Christ in Scripture. He was beloved of his father, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected and betrayed by his own, sold for silver, falsely accused and condemned though innocent, placed between two prisoners one of whom lived and one of whom died, and then suddenly raised from the lowest place to the highest position in the kingdom. Every stage of Joseph’s story points forward to Christ. And Joseph’s story began at seventeen. The number of victory over judgment was also the number at which the suffering that leads to victory began. Seventeen did not just mark the arrival at Ararat. It also marked the beginning of the descent into the pit. The two appearances of seventeen together form one complete message: the path to victory goes through suffering, and the one who endures the pit and the prison will one day rest the ark on the mountain.

When we hold both appearances of seventeen together and lay them over the seventeen peace offering animals of Numbers 7, the picture becomes breathtaking. The peace that Christ established was not a peace that bypassed suffering. It was a peace that was purchased through the deepest suffering ever endured by any living being. Isaiah 53:5 says: “Upon Him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with His wounds we are healed.” The chastisement that brought peace. The wounds that brought healing. The suffering that produced the shalom. Joseph went into rejection & sufferings at seventeen so that eventually Pharaoh could say “there is no one as discerning and wise as you” and place the ring on his finger. Christ went into the tomb so that the Father could raise Him and give Him the name above every name.

Philippians 2:8-9 traces this exact movement: “He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted Him and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name.” The humbling first. The exaltation second. The pit first. The throne second. Seventeen peace offerings on the altar of dedication are declaring this sequence. The peace of God does not arrive without the journey through suffering. The ark rests on Ararat on the seventeenth, but it got there by riding the waters of judgment for months. The peace that fills the altar of Numbers 7 with seventeen animals is the peace that came through the cross, the burial, and the resurrection of the one who said “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

The seventeen peace offering animals speak directly to the new creation believer who is still in the middle of the journey; still between the pit and the throne, still riding the flood waters before the ark has rested on the mountain. The message of seventeen is not only that peace was purchased. It is that the suffering through which the peace came was not wasted, was not random, and was not the end. Joseph did not know at seventeen that the dreams he had been given would one day be literally fulfilled with his brothers bowing before him in Egypt. All he knew at seventeen was the rejection, hatred sufferings, the darkness, and the sound of the merchants’ caravan heading south. But the seventeen of his age was already carrying the message of Ararat: the ark will rest. The waters will recede. The new beginning will come. Victory is on the other side of this judgment.

Hebrews 12:2 says: “Looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.” For the joy set before Him. He endured the cross because He could see Ararat from inside the flood.

He endured the pit because He could see Egypt’s throne from inside the slavery. And the seventeen animals of peace that each tribal leader laid before Yahweh at the altar of dedication were a seventeen-fold declaration that the suffering which preceded the peace was worth it, that the judgment which the cross absorbed was real, and that the peace which followed is genuine, established, and eternal.

We carry this truth on our shoulders today. Whatever pit we are in, whatever flood we are riding, whatever season of suffering has preceded the peace we are still waiting to arrive at; the seventeen animals on the altar are for us.

The ark rested on the seventeenth. The dreamer at seventeen eventually wore the ring of Pharaoh. And the one who was crucified in judgment rose in victory and now gives His peace to all who come through Him. The number on the peace offering altar is seventeen. The peace is certain. The rest will come.

title: Prayer
text: Yahweh, the LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge (Psalm 46:7). You are the God who rested the ark on solid ground on the seventeenth day; the God who brought the flood to its end and established a new beginning on the other side of judgment. We thank You that the seventeen peace offerings on the altar of dedication declare the same truth: suffering leads to victory, judgment gives way to peace, and the one who goes into the pit at seventeen comes out to wear the ring of authority. We thank You for Christ, who endured the cross for the joy set before Him, who went through the flood of Yahweh’s judgment on our sin and came to rest in resurrection on the other side, establishing a peace that will never be broken. For all of us who are still between the pit and the throne, still riding the flood before the ark has settled; help us to fix our eyes on the seventeenth, on the mountain where the ark rests, on the peace that is already secured even while the waters are still high. In Christ’s name, amen.
